definition: Moralistic means quick to lecture others about right and wrong; preachy.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word moralistic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know moralistic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The hiking forum's most moralistic member answers every gear thread with a short sermon on the vanity of ultralight equipment and the decay of self-reliance.
A principled person holds firm standards quietly — well short of moralistic, which cannot hold a standard without delivering it as a lecture.
Self-righteous goes further than moralistic: the lecturing continues, and the lecturer has privately concluded that no one else could possibly measure up.

Judgmental means quick to condemn — the verdict arrives fast, sticks, and needs no words at all. Moralistic adds the sermon on top of the verdict: the moralistic person must also deliver the lecture about right and wrong. Every moralistic uncle is judgmental, but a judgmental one might only glare.

Sermonizing is the act itself — delivering little moral lectures no one requested, one speech at a time. Moralistic names the habit of mind behind them: the standing urge to grade everyone's conduct as right or wrong. Sermonizing is what a moralistic person is caught doing out loud.

Debates about the morality of zoos have redrawn enclosure designs on every continent.
Moralistic means quick to lecture others about right and wrong; preachy.
What began as a cooking show turned moralistic by season three: each recipe now arrives with a little homily on thankfulness, waste, and the character of people who buy pre-chopped onions.
Moralistic is more precise than 'strict' or 'serious' because it points at the lecturing itself: a moralistic person turns every topic into a lesson about right and wrong, invited or not.
Being moral is living by principles; being moralistic is preaching them at the table.
Moralistic is almost always a complaint — about narrators, uncles, and editorials that lecture.
Don't confuse it with moral (actually good) or with careful ethical reasoning.

Among its unit-mates, solipsistic and sophomoric describe other ways a speaker wears on you: the solipsistic one sees only himself, the sophomoric one shows off, and the moralistic one grades your soul over dessert.

The community garden's newsletter used to be four lines about watering schedules until Harold took over as editor.

Now each issue opens with a column in which Harold grades the membership's conduct: who hoarded the good compost, who let their zucchini shade a neighbor's peppers, and what these lapses reveal about character.
Even the calendar section is moralistic, pausing between dates to remind readers that a borrowed trowel returned late is a small dishonesty.
Members mostly shrug, since Harold's facts are accurate and his own plot is tidy.
But several have quietly asked whether a note about the June potluck really needs a paragraph on the duty we owe one another.
